question: What is a transformer?
answer: A transformer is the kind of model behind today's chatbots. It turns text into numbers, passes them through a stack of layers where each word gathers information from the words before it, and ends with a score for every possible next piece of text.

question: How does a model write a whole answer?
answer: One piece at a time. The model gives every possible next piece a chance, one piece is picked, it is added to the text, and the model guesses again. Chatbots repeat this hundreds of times to write a reply.

question: Why can the same text give a different answer each time?
answer: The model gives chances, not one answer. The next piece is drawn at random using those chances, so two runs can pick different pieces and then go different ways. The temperature controls how adventurous the draw is. Greedy decoding always takes the top guess and gives the same text every time.

question: Why does the model read tokens instead of letters or whole words?
answer: Whole words would need an endless list, and new or rare words would be missing. Single letters would make texts very long. Tokens sit in between. Common words are one token, and rare words are built from smaller pieces, so any text can still be written.

sources.quote: making the NMT model capable of open-vocabulary translation by encoding rare and unknown words as sequences of subword units

question: Does the model know what words mean?
answer: Nobody tells it. The model only sees token ids, and it learns numbers for each one that help it guess the next token. Along the way, words used in similar ways end up with similar numbers, such as girl and boy. Whether that counts as knowing what a word means is a question this site leaves open. What it shows is what the numbers do.

question: Why does attention divide the scores by the square root of the list length?
answer: A dot product adds up one product per number, so with longer lists the scores tend to get bigger. Very big scores make softmax put almost all the weight on one token, and then training learns very slowly. Dividing by the square root of the length keeps the scores in a range where softmax still spreads its weight. In our model the lists have 32 numbers, so the scores are divided by about 5.66.

sources.quote: We suspect that for large values of d_k, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients.

question: Why can a token not look at the tokens after it?
answer: The model learns by guessing each next token. If a token could see the tokens after it, it could copy the answer instead of learning to guess. The causal mask hides later tokens by setting their scores to minus infinity, so their weight after softmax is exactly 0.

sources.quote: We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property.

question: How does the model know the order of the words?
answer: Attention on its own does not see order. So the model also learns a list of numbers for each place in the text and adds it to each token's list. The same word then looks a little different in a different place.

sources.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

question: Do the attention weights explain why the model chose a word?
answer: Not on their own. They show where a head looked, not why the model decided what it did. Researchers disagree about how much the weights can tell you, so treat them as a clue to test, not an explanation.

sources.quote: We find that they largely do not.
such a claim depends on one's definition of explanation

question: Why does each layer add to a token's numbers instead of replacing them?
answer: Adding keeps what came before, so nothing earlier is lost and each layer only has to learn a change. This also makes deep stacks of layers much easier to train.

sources.quote: We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions.

question: Why is the model on this site so small?
answer: So it runs in your browser and every number can be shown. It has about 1.3 million learned numbers, 4 layers and a vocabulary of 4,096 tokens. It was trained on simple children's stories, and research has shown that models this small can still write fluent short stories.

sources.quote: We show that TinyStories can be used to train and evaluate LMs that are much smaller than the state-of-the-art models (below 10 million total parameters)

question: How is this different from a chat model?
answer: A chat model follows the same plan with far more layers and learned numbers, trained on far more text. It is then trained further to follow instructions, using examples written by people and their ratings of its answers. This site covers the plan they share.

sources.quote: we show an avenue for aligning language models with user intent on a wide range of tasks by fine-tuning with human feedback

question: Does this site send what I type anywhere?
answer: No. The model runs in your browser, so your text stays on your device. The playground does put your text in the page's address, so a link you share carries it.
